summary:
Chad's penal code, in force since 1 August 2017, criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults under Article 354, carrying three months to two years' imprisonment and fines of 50,000 to 500,000 CFA francs (roughly 89 to 885 US dollars). A trans visitor whose conduct or relationship is read as same-sex under the provision falls within its reach. The National Assembly adopted the code on 12 December 2016 by 111 votes to one, with four abstentions.

Article 360, in Chapter III on sexual offences against minors, punishes a person who without violence maintains a sexual relationship or practices sexual touching with a person of the same sex under eighteen years of age with one to three years' imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 500,000 francs (about 177 to 885 US dollars).

Chad has no legal gender recognition. There is no pathway for a trans person to amend sex markers on official documents, so a visitor's travel documents cannot be brought into line with their lived gender under Chadian law.

Because same-sex conduct is criminalised, police and prosecutors refuse to investigate or prosecute crimes committed against LGBTQ+ people, and local civil society members say dozens of LGBTQ+ people are held in prison under the pretext of other charges. The only provision in Chadian law that addresses violence targeting someone for their sexual orientation is Article 350(i), which imposes ten to twenty years' imprisonment when rape is committed because of the victim's sexual orientation. There is no general legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Enforcement predates the 2017 code. In 2013 two men were arrested in Abéché for celebrating their wedding, before the penal code formally outlawed homosexuality; the bar was ordered closed for two years, both men were fined and initially given two-year prison sentences, and those sentences were suspended on appeal after community outcry. Religious groups, women's groups and youth associations petitioned the government to punish the men.

Official hostility to the law's targets is on the record. Former Prime Minister Delwa Kassiré Coumakoye defended the 2017 criminalisation on religious grounds, saying homosexuality is condemned by all religions.

Social attitudes are hostile. LGBTQ+ people are viewed as threats to family, procreation and marriage, and homosexuality is perceived as a Western invention. In a 2024 survey, 15 percent of Chadians felt their local area would be a good place for gay and lesbian people to live. LGBTQ+ people in Chad continue to hide their identity to protect their safety.

Healthcare access is affected. Men who have sex with men are unlikely to be able to donate blood, not because of a formal ban but because of discrimination and hostility encountered when accessing healthcare.

No law formally restricts LGBTQ+ people's freedom of expression, association or peaceful assembly, but discrimination and marginalisation limit these rights in practice.
tangentialFactors:
Chad's 2017 criminalisation belongs to a wider wave of conservative advocacy in the region: comparable attempts failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda in the same period while succeeding in Chad and Nigeria.

Before the 2017 code, Chadian law prohibited but did not define 'unnatural acts', and the 2010 US State Department human rights report recorded no evidence that the provision was used against LGBT persons that year. The same report noted no known LGBT organisations in the country and few reports of violence, with most people living discreetly because of social strictures. That baseline describes the pre-2017 climate and not the current statute.
localsOnly:
Chad does not recognise same-sex couples, so a couple cannot adopt children jointly. A single person may adopt, but the process requires a social services investigation that includes an inquiry into the applicant's moral standing, which can be used as grounds to refuse. That route can be turned against LGBTQ+ applicants.

Despite constitutional universal suffrage, LGBTQ+ Chadians are often denied voter registration by local authorities.

LGBTQ+ people in Chad have difficulty obtaining housing, employment and government services.

Chadian activists report that social and familial pressure is used to coerce LGBTQ+ people into changing their sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression.
outOfScopeNotes:
The figure of dozens of LGBTQ+ people imprisoned under other charges comes from local civil society members and is not independently corroborated in the source inventory.

The 2024 attitudinal survey is reported as a single measure; the source does not describe its sample, method or margin of error.

Whether Article 350(i) has ever been applied in a prosecution is not stated in the sources.

The source inventory contains no trans-specific violence statistics for Chad, so no comparison against the country's general homicide rate can be made.
